----Respondents
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Gaurav Ranka
For Respondent(s) : Mr. Saurabh Maheshwari
 Hon'Ble Mr. Justice Arun Monga
Order 14/03/2024
1. Petitioners/employer (department of Medical & Health) is before this Court assailing an award dated 08.08.2005 rendered by learned Labour Court, Bhilwara.
An order dated 17.10.2002 terminating services of respondent No. 1 - Smt. Manju Berwa was held to be illegal by the learned Labour Court.

Consequently, department has been directed to take the Respondent No. 1 back in service as Multi Purpose Worker (MPW Female/Workman) on contractual basis, as was the position when her services were terminated vide order dated 17.10.2002 passed by the Department.
2. Relevant facts of the case are that the respondent No.1 was engaged as MPW (Female) on a fixed salary of Rs.3,500/- vide office order dated 07.07.2000 (Annexure-3).

While in service,
[2024:RJ-JD:12273] (2 of 8) [CW-3809/2006] respondent No.1 got implicated in a criminal case arising out of an FIR No.302/2002 under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 384 & 120B of the IPC.
She was allegedly falsely involved in the criminal case, which is stated to have cropped up out of some family dispute.
Be that as it may, she was arrested by the police and presented before the learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bhilwara on 18.07.2002.
She was then remanded to judicial custody.
Thereafter, respondent No.1 was enlarged on bail on 26.07.2002.
After getting bail, she approached her employer for resuming her duty, but the petitioners vide order dated 17.10.2002 terminated her services.
She thus approached the learned Labour Court.
Subsequently, during the pendency of the instant writ proceedings, in the criminal trial arising out of the FIR, ibid, she was State And Anr vs Smt.Manju Berwa And Anr. ...

4. Learned counsel for the petitioners would foremost argue that case of the petitioners is squarely covered by a judgment of Supreme Court rendered in Satish Chandra Yadav v. Union of India & Ors.

5. He would further argue that letters/notices were sent to her at her residence but she was since in judicial custody she did not turn up for duty.
That being the position, the present is not at all a case where relief of reinstatement should have been granted by the learned Labour Court.
He would further argue that the burden of proving the facts stated in the claim petition lies on the [2024:RJ-JD:12273] (3 of 8) [CW-3809/2006] respondent No.1.
However, the learned Labour Court has thus wrongly granted the relief to her.

6. Per contra, learned counsel for respondent No.1 would urge that the petitioners, without conducting any enquiry, in an arbitrary manner passed the termination order merely on the basis of a newspaper report that respondent No.1 had been arrested.

He would further argue that, realising their mistake, the petitioners on the one hand vide a communication dated 30.07.2002 directed to reinstate the respondent No.1, but on the other hand, services of respondent No.1 were abruptly terminated.
7. He would further argue that on account of compelling circumstances, respondent No.1 could not attend the duties and, as such, it cannot be construed as wilful absence.

Reliance was placed on Supreme Court judgments rendered in Krushnakant B. Parmer v. Union of India (UOI) & Ors. :
(2012) 3 SCC 178 and Chhel Singh v. M.G.B. Gramin Bank : (2014) 13 SCC 166.
8.

He would argue that the respondent No.1 has not committed any act, which could be considered to be moral turpitude.

He would also rely on the judgment of this Court rendered in Sanjay Dadich v.
State of Rajasthan & Ors. : S.B. CWP No.6869/2007, decided on 17.10.2023 (Jaipur Bench).

She did not remain absent from the work at her own will but due to circumstances beyond her control caused by an act of State.
The order of termination of her services was passed in violation of Section 25(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
10. As regards the impugned award herein, learned counsel for respondent No.1 would submit that the same has been rightly rendered in accordance with law.

Court, inter alia, for the following reasons:
(a) The termination order dated 17.10.2002 does not reveal that how the claimant has committed offence of moral turpitude while performing her duties.

(b) Learned Labour Court has rightly observed that mere unsubstantiated accusation on the claimant/workman for being involved in alleged conspiracy, she has been terminated without conducting any disciplinary enquiry.
(c) The termination of services of the claimant is stigmatic and is against the law as it has been done without giving her any opportunity of hearing before passing termination order.

(d) Learned Labour Court also rightly observed that the absence of the claimant from the duty cannot be considered to be wilful absence and the appointment of the respondent No.1 cannot be considered as temporary appointment as she has been performing her duties from 07.07.2000 to 17.07.2002 and the appointment of the claimant has been through selection, as is mentioned in the appointment order dated 07.07.2000.
[2024:RJ-JD:12273] (5 of 8) [CW-3809/2006]
11.

Learned counsel for respondent No.1 would further argue that during pendency of instant writ proceeding the respondent No.1 had preferred an application before this Court under Section 17-B of the Industrial Disputes Act seeking direction to the petitioners to pay the full wages last drawn by respondent No.1.
The said application was allowed by this Court vide order dated 02.03.2007 directing the petitioners to pay full wages to the respondent No.1 as has been last drawn by her.
He would argue that it is pertinent to mention here that the said order dated 02.03.2007 has not been challenged by the petitioners.

12. Learned counsel for respondent No.1 would further argue that similarly situated persons have been made permanent/regularized on the job but due to pendency of the present writ petition she has not been able to join her duties since the year 2002.
13. He would argue that in the criminal case filed against respondent No.1, vide acquittal order dated 03.12.2011 it has been observed that no evidence was found against respondent No.1.
14. Learned counsel for respondent No.1 would also argue that workman has not been reinstated since 2005 despite an order passed by learned Labour Court.
He would argue that pendency of present writ petition and not letting the respondent No.1 be reinstated is a classic example of "justice delayed is justice denied".
Now she is in advanced age.
She is also entitled to the benefit of due determination of the seniority and pay scale.

sentences.text: I shall now proceed to render my opinion on the rival contentions as noted herein above and record reasons thereof.

16. First and foremost, from a communication dated 30.07.2002 written by Chief Medical & Health Officer, Bhilwara it emerges that the petitioners themselves had at one stage passed a favorable recommendation, whereby Dy. Medical & Health Officer was instructed that she be taken back on duty but by not paying the wages for the days she was absent from work.
It was further instructed that a warning may be given to her that in future such absence from duty would result in adverse consequences.

It is rather intriguing that on one hand such favorable recommendation was made and, on the other, instead of complying with the same the writ petition has been filed by the same very department through the same officer assailing the impugned award.
17.

Further, it transpires that the same very officer, who had recommended that respondent No.1 be taken back in service vide his earlier communication dated 30.07.2002 but subsequently as a bolt from the blue passed the termination order dated 17.10.2002 on the ground that the respondent No.1 had remained wilfully absent and she had committed moral turpitude in view of being involved in criminal proceedings.
18.

Having given my thought to the aforesaid arguments and after careful consideration thereof, I am of the view that neither the impugned award dated 08.08.2005 rendered by learned Labour Court, Bhilwara suffers from any material irregularity in law nor any misappreciation of the evidence.

Even otherwise, the findings written, based on the cogent evidence adduced by both [2024:RJ-JD:12273] (7 of 8) [CW-3809/2006] the sides, do not suffer from any kind of perversity so as to warrant interference of this Court.
19. Further more, the petitioner department is clearly indulging in approbating and reprobating.
Inasmuch as, on one hand same officer recommended taking respondent No. 1 back in service, on the other hand making a complete somersault, termination order was passed few days thereafter.
Such a conduct to say the least is certainly not appreciable if not deplorable.
20. As regards the back wages, the services of respondent No.1 were terminated vide order dated 17.10.2002.
Since then, she did not actually work on the post.
Payment of colossal amount of arrears to her for over 21 years without having worked does not seem just and fair.
However, a co-ordinate Bench of this Court (then ceased up the matter) vide order dated 02.03.2007 directed the petitioners to pay full back wages to the respondent-workman.

The said order being apposite is reproduced herein below:-
"By an application being I.A. No.427/2007 under section 17-B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the respondent- workman seeks a direction to the petitioner State to pay the full wages last drawn by her.
Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case
, the application is allowed and the petitioner employer is directed to pay the full wages last drawn by the respondent-workman."

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is pertinent to note here that the aforesaid directions/order dated 02.03.2007 has attained finality as the same was not challenged by the petitioners.

In the overall circumstances of the case,
the arrears are confined to 100% of the full back wages upto 02.03.2007 when the directions to that extent were issued to the petitioners.

For the subsequent period commencing w.e.f. 03.03.2007 till date arrears are confined to [2024:RJ-JD:12273] (8 of 8) [CW-3809/2006] 50% of the wages to be calculated on the basis of last drawn salary by the respondent No.1.

The financial benefits of respondent No.1 have though been confined but she shall be entitled to all the notional benefits with effect from year 2002, when her services were terminated, including the seniority.
If found eligible on parity with her counterparts, she would be accorded regularization in accordance thereof.
She shall be deemed to be in service with effect from the same date as her similarly situated other contractual counterparts were recruited and given benefit of seniority thereof.
Arrears of back wages be paid alongwith interest as per the applicable rate according to the service rules.
22. Necessary exercise be carried out within a period of 30 days from the date respondent No.1 approaches the petitioners with web print of the instant order.

The petitioners are directed to take the respondent No.1 back in service on parity with her counterparts, who at the relevant time continued to be in service by extending their contract from time to time.
23. The impugned award dated 08.08.2005 rendered by learned Labour Court, Bhilwara is modified as above and the writ petition is disposed of accordingly.

(ARUN MONGA),J 1-AK Chouhan/-
